newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico seen big loser in fight over U.S. envoy.
newsitem.headline: Mexico seen big loser in fight over U.S. envoy.

text.p: As Washington bickers over who should be the next U.S. ambassador to Mexico, in Mexico only one thing counts -- an empty chair in the most important diplomatic post in the country.

It may be the latest summer intrigue for Washington political junkies, but the struggle by conservative Sen. Jesse Helms to block the nomination of fellow Republican William Weld is expected by Mexicans to end up dealing them a diplomatic black eye.

"The big loser will be Mexico because we'll be without an ambassador for six months ... and the embassy will be left rudderless," Denise Dresser, a political analyst who has written on Weld's nomination, told Reuters.

Weld, who has the backing of (U.S.) President Bill Clinton, resigned as governor of Massachusetts on Tuesday to pursue the ambassadorship, but he has run into a brick wall in the form of Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.

The confrontation has become a tug-of-war between Republican leaders opposing Weld's nomination and Clinton. Dresser said the credibility of Clinton's commitment to Mexico was at stake if he failed to win the nomination.
"It would show Clinton still views Mexico as an afterthought and that he's not going to win many wars on Mexico in his second term," she said.

She noted the vacancy occurs as Mexico faces a new round of U.S. scrutiny on its drugs record in September -- always a time of raw cross-border nerves when a U.S. ambassador is called upon to calm tempers on Capitol Hill and in Mexico.

In February, the U.S. Congress came close to blocking the White House's certification of Mexico as an ally in the war on drugs. That fight, with Helms at the forefront of the anti-Mexico lobby, strained bilateral relations.
If no ambassador is installed by September, the White House report to the Senate on Mexico's drugs record would be the second major event missed in months.
In July Mexico went through landmark Congressional elections without a U.S. ambassador, following the departure of former envoy James Jones in June.
A defeat for Weld would also mark a victory for Helms, a long-time bugbear of Mexico who has frequently condemned the country for its drugs record.

"I would think very few people in Mexico would consider Helms a friend or a benign influence," a former Mexican diplomat with long experience of U.S.-Mexican affairs told Reuters. "Many feel it's time to put him in his place."
Mexicans have been stunned by Helms' almost single-handed ability to block the White House on the nomination, and the showdown has raised a sympathy here for Weld that is rare for a U.S. envoy.
"Any enemy of Helms is a friend of Mexico," Dresser said.
Other qualities mentioned in Mexico: The former governor speaks Spanish, a major plus after his predecessor battled with the language for four years.

He also has a temperament that Mexicans say will play well south of the border. Helms has objected to his support of marijuana as medicine, and described him as a man not of ambassador quality who is "a little loose with his lips".

But Mexican newspaper El Norte this week celebrated his antics as Massachusetts governor, such as his decision to dive into Boston's River Charles in his clothes to celebrate passage of a law about clean water.
"We don't know if William Weld would be the best U.S. ambassador in Mexico, but we can say without a doubt he would be the most fun," it said in an editorial.
